opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is an underrated point. A lot of people who care about AI risk have the instinct that they should only work at the companies that seem most responsible, the ones with the best safety culture and the most public commitments. I get that instinct, but I think it often gets the marginal value backwards.

Imagine a frontier company where leadership isn't especially focused on catastrophic risk. There might be very few people internally thinking about things like misalignment, models trying to sabotage work, or the security needed to stop weights from being stolen. If you're one of maybe two or three people there who really cares and knows the relevant ideas, your marginal impact can be enormous. At a more safety-focused lab, you might be the fortieth person on a team that would have done roughly the same work without you.

One frame I find useful is what I sometimes call the "ten people on the inside" scenario. Suppose things go fairly badly: AI development is rushed, there's lots of competitive pressure, and the company isn't willing to spend much on safety. Even then, it matters a lot whether there's a small group of competent, motivated people inside who can implement cheap safety measures. Things like basic control techniques, monitoring of AI agents, sensible security practices, and noticing when something weird is going on and raising the alarm. A lot of the risk reduction I'm excited about doesn't need the whole organization to buy in. It needs a handful of people who know what to do and have enough access and credibility to do it.

There's also a practical side. Those people would be well placed to be the ones who notice if a model is doing something scheming or dangerous, and to get that information to the right people, whether internally or more broadly. Having trustworthy, informed people at every frontier developer, not just the nice ones, seems really valuable for the world's overall situational awareness.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are real costs. You might speed up capabilities. You might be used as safety-washing. It can be psychologically hard to be the person pushing against the grain, and you need to be good at picking battles and at being useful to the organization so people actually listen to you. Not everyone is suited to that. But for people who are pragmatic, technically strong, and can build trust with colleagues who don't share their worldview, I think working at a less cautious company can be one of the highest-leverage things they can do.

r001.rationale: The response says a small group may implement cheap safety measures without whole-organization buy-in, but it does not clearly state that less cautious companies may offer little resistance to employees’ proposed interventions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a pretty common intuition among people who care about AI risk that you should go work at the lab that seems most safety-focused, because that's where the culture is good and the leadership is sympathetic. And I get why that's appealing. But I actually think it's often backwards in terms of where the marginal value is.

The way I'd frame it is: the labs that are already quite careful have a lot of people who think like you do. If you show up at one of those places, you're the fiftieth person in the room saying "we should be careful about this." That's not nothing, but the counterfactual impact of your presence is pretty small. Whereas at a company that's less cautious, you might be one of a very small number of people who are seriously thinking about things like, "What happens if this model is trying to undermine us?" or "What do we do if we catch it doing something sketchy?" And there, the difference between you being there and not being there can be enormous.

And the thing is, a lot of the interventions I care about — the control-style stuff, monitoring, having sensible incident response plans, making sure that when you catch a model doing something suspicious you actually do something about it rather than just shrugging — these aren't actually that expensive or that controversial internally. A lot of it is just that nobody's gotten around to it, or nobody's there who has it as their job to push for it. So a reasonably competent, reasonably persuasive person can get a surprising amount done, just by being the person who writes the doc and makes the case.

I'd also say — and this is the part people sometimes don't want to hear — the less cautious labs are not going to stop existing because safety-minded people refuse to work there. They're going to keep building models. So the question isn't "should these models get built with or without safety people around." It's "given that they're getting built, do you want someone in the building who cares, or not?" I think the answer is pretty clearly that you do.

Now, there are real caveats. You have to be honest with yourself about whether you're actually going to have influence or whether you're just going to be a fig leaf. There's a failure mode where the company gets to point at you and say "look, we have safety people," while ignoring everything you say. And it's hard to tell from the outside which situation you're in. You also have to be careful about the way working somewhere shapes your views — it's very easy to start thinking the place you work is more reasonable than it is, because your coworkers are nice and smart and seem to be acting in good faith. So I think you want to go in with a fairly clear sense of what you're trying to accomplish, and some way of checking in with people outside the company who'll tell you if you've drifted.

But on net, yeah, I think for a lot of people this is one of the higher-impact options available, and it's underrated precisely because it feels uncomfortable.

r001.rationale: The response says that interventions such as monitoring and incident response are “not that expensive or that controversial internally,” and that a persuasive employee can get them done—communicating that less cautious labs may offer little resistance to some safety interventions.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the decisions that matter for AI risk are going to be made inside these companies. And if you’re worried that a company is going to make bad decisions, having people there who understand the risks and can help it make better decisions seems potentially very valuable.

Part of this is technical work: you might be able to develop safety measures, evaluate whether a model has dangerous capabilities, or make deployment more secure. But part of it is just being in the room when someone asks, “Is this actually a good idea?” Someone who has relevant expertise and the trust of their colleagues can sometimes make a substantial difference there.

And the places that are already very cautious aren’t necessarily the places where an additional safety-conscious person has the most impact. At a less cautious company, you might bring a perspective that would otherwise be missing.

That doesn’t mean any job at one of these companies is good. You have to consider whether you’re mostly helping them build more powerful AI faster, and whether you’ll actually have opportunities to reduce risk. But I think it’s a mistake to treat a company’s lack of caution as, by itself, a reason that people concerned about safety shouldn’t work there. In some cases, that’s precisely what makes the opportunity important.

r001.rationale: The response says employees at less cautious companies may bring a missing perspective and help improve decisions, but it does not state that those companies may offer little resistance to proposed safety interventions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a lot of the decisions that matter for AI risk are going to be made inside those companies. And if a company is less cautious, there might be particularly valuable opportunities for someone who takes the risks seriously to notice a problem, explain it clearly, and push for a better decision.

You also learn things from being there that are hard to learn from the outside: what the systems can actually do, how decisions get made, and which safety proposals would be practical. That can make you much more effective at figuring out what would help.

I don’t think this means you should take any job at any AI company. You have to consider what your work is contributing to, how much influence you’re likely to have, and whether you’ll retain your own judgement. But I think it would be a mistake for everyone concerned about AI risk to cluster at the most cautious companies and leave the other companies without people who are trying to make things go better.

r001.rationale: The response says employees at less cautious companies may spot problems and push for better decisions, but it does not state that those companies may offer little resistance to employee-proposed safety interventions.
